extracted.intended_audience: state regulators (CARB), vehicle manufacturers, environmental and industry stakeholders, agency attorneys, and other parties interested in Clean Air Act section 209(b) waiver decisions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria EPA uses to evaluate California requests for waiver of Clean Air Act preemption for motor vehicle emission standards under section 209(b). Covers the statutory three-part inquiry, procedural steps, burdens and standards of proof, and relevant judicial deference principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Review (limit to section 209(b)(1) questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should limit its inquiry to the specific findings identified in section 209(b)(1) of the Clean Air Act; matters not specified in the statute are not proper grounds for denying a waiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA will not engage in probing substantive review or second-guess California's policy choices; arguments such as whether a requirement yields only marginal air-quality improvement relative to its costs are not legally pertinent to the section 209 decision so long as the California requirement is consistent with section 202(a) and more stringent than federal requirements. Supported by case law (e.g., Ford v. EPA, MEMA I) and prior waiver decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of Proof — who must prove denial criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Opponents of a California waiver request bear the burden of showing that the statutory criteria for denial under section 209(b)(1) have been met; California's determinations are presumed to satisfy the waiver requirements when presented to the Administrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites MEMA I: opponents must persuade the Administrator that the waiver should be denied. California must present its regulations and findings at the hearing; the Administrator evaluates the record but the burden of proving denial rests with challengers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of Proof — variable and fact-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of proof the Administrator applies varies with the specific finding involved and the nature/risk of error; evidence must pass a threshold test of materiality before being assessed against the applicable standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court guidance (MEMA I) indicates standards vary: for example, to deny a waiver on protectiveness grounds based on enforcement procedures, there must be 'clear and compelling evidence' that procedures undermine protectiveness. For other findings, courts have applied standards up to preponderance; EPA need not decide a single fixed standard for all situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to California's Policy Judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA will give substantial deference to California's determinations and policy judgments in adopting its motor vehicle emission regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute and legislative history show Congress intended limited federal review and broad California discretion; EPA practice and case law support leaving ambiguous and controversial public-policy matters to California's judgment. EPA must avoid second-guessing so long as statutory criteria are satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA's Administrative Process (notice, comment, hearing, docket)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA will provide notice of the waiver request, solicit public comments and requests for hearing, and maintain a public docket containing documents relied upon in making the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: EPA published notice of opportunity for public hearing and comment (requested comments on the three statutory criteria). If no hearing requests/comments are received, EPA may not hold a hearing. Docket materials available at regulations.gov and in EPA reading room; Confidential Business Information excluded from public docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protectiveness Determination Criterion — section 209(b)(1)(A)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must deny a waiver if the Administrator finds that California's protectiveness determination—that its standards, in the aggregate, are at least as protective of public health and welfare as federal standards—was arbitrary and capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To deny on this ground, there must be clear and convincing evidence that California's protectiveness finding was unreasonable. EPA's review is narrow and confined to whether there's convincing evidence California's finding was arbitrary and capricious; EPA previously found that CARB's protectiveness determination for the Phase 1 GHG Regulation was reasonable and not arbitrary or capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for State Standards to Meet Compelling and Extraordinary Conditions — section 209(b)(1)(B)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's inquiry under this criterion is whether California needs its own motor vehicle emission control program (the program as a whole) to meet compelling and extraordinary conditions, not whether the specific standards at issue are individually necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA interprets 'such State standards' to mean the motor vehicle program generally. Evidence of California's continuing geographic/climatic conditions, severe air quality problems (e.g., South Coast, San Joaquin Valley), and legislative findings (Global Warming Solutions Act, executive orders) support the need. EPA will deny only if it finds California does not need such state standards to meet compelling/extraordinary conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with Section 202(a) — section 209(b)(1)(C)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must deny a waiver if it finds that California's standards and accompanying enforcement procedures are not consistent with section 202(a), which requires adequate lead time for development and application of relevant technology considering compliance cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination focuses on technological feasibility, adequacy of lead time, cost of compliance within the time, and whether test procedures conflict so manufacturers cannot comply with both federal and California requirements using the same test vehicle. Opponents must show technological infeasibility or test-procedure inconsistency; EPA found no evidence of infeasibility or test conflicts for the Phase 1 GHG Regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of Accompanying Enforcement Procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluates whether California's accompanying enforcement procedures (1) impact the state's protectiveness determination and (2) are consistent with section 202(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MEMA I articulates these two specific findings when enforcement procedures are at issue. To deny based on enforcement procedures undermining protectiveness, challengers must supply clear and compelling evidence. Enforcement procedures may also be reviewed for test-procedure conflicts that would prevent dual compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality Threshold for Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA will 'consider all evidence that passes the threshold test of materiality' and thereafter assess such material evidence against the applicable standard of proof for the finding at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopts MEMA I guidance: only evidence meeting a materiality threshold is weighed; the Administrator must not ignore material evidence or substitute unsupported assumptions, or the decision risks being set aside as arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'Deemed-to-Comply' Federal Certification as Compliance Mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA recognizes and may consider California provisions that allow manufacturers to demonstrate compliance with California standards by showing compliance with corresponding federal regulations (e.g., submitting EPA Certificate of Conformity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CARB's Phase 1 GHG Regulation contains 'deemed to comply' provisions allowing engine manufacturers to demonstrate compliance for 2014–2022 model years by submitting EPA's Certificate of Conformity; such provisions can alleviate concerns about test-procedure conflict and feasibility and are relevant to EPA's consistency and protectiveness analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on Grounds for Denial (matters not legally pertinent)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA will not deny a waiver based on considerations that are not among the statute's enumerated grounds, such as policy preferences, marginal cost-benefit judgments, or arguments outside section 209(b)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA has stated that issues like whether a requirement is an unwise exercise of regulatory power or yields marginal air-quality improvement relative to cost are not proper bases for denial if standards meet the statutory criteria. The D.C. Circuit has upheld this narrow scope of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality and Judicial Review Procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: A waiver decision that is a final action of national applicability/nationwide scope is subject to judicial review only in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit within the statutory deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: EPA's decision granting the Phase 1 GHG waiver is final, and petitions for review must be filed by the date specified (e.g., February 27, 2017); judicial review cannot be obtained in subsequent enforcement proceedings pursuant to section 307(b)(2).
